relationship_to_restored_text: Interpretive contemplative layer aligned by verse. This does not replace the source-audited restored translation.

verses.mystical_translation: After years of drought, the word finally turns toward rain and confrontation.
Elijah moves toward Ahab while Samaria remains crushed by famine.
Inside Ahab's house, Obadiah quietly reveres YHWH.
When prophets are hunted, he hides one hundred people and sustains them with scarce bread and water.
The king searches for grass to save royal horses and mules while the land starves.
Ahab and Obadiah divide the dry land between them.
The hidden resister meets the fugitive prophet on the road.
Elijah asks him to carry dangerous news to the king.
Obadiah immediately names the likely cost: his own death.
Ahab's search has pressured whole nations to swear they did not hide Elijah.
The messenger is asked to announce what the royal hunt could not find.
Obadiah fears Elijah will vanish and leave him exposed to execution.
He reminds Elijah of the lives he preserved through secret food and shelter.
His fear is not lack of faith but knowledge of the regime.
Elijah swears he will appear before Ahab that day.
Obadiah takes the risk, and the king comes to meet the prophet.
Ahab calls Elijah the source of Israel's trouble.
Elijah returns responsibility to the royal house and its abandoned covenant.
A national gathering is summoned around competing prophetic institutions.
The king gathers people and prophets at Carmel.
Elijah asks the people to stop limping between loyalties; silence answers him.
He experiences himself as one against hundreds, though others have been hidden and preserved.
Two bulls become the bodies upon which religious proof will be staged.
The people accept fire as the proposed test of Divine reality.
The larger group prepares first.
They call, dance, and wait through the morning without answer.
Elijah turns their silence into public mockery.
They intensify the ritual by cutting their own bodies until blood flows.
The long effort produces no voice or response.
Elijah gathers the people near and repairs a broken altar.
Twelve stones remember a people larger than the divided kingdoms.
The altar and trench are built in the name of YHWH.
The second animal is cut, arranged, and drenched with scarce water.
Water is poured again and again.
The trench fills until the altar stands inside abundance amid drought.
Elijah asks that his service and the Divine identity be made known.
He asks not only for fire but for hearts to turn.
Fire consumes sacrifice, wood, stone, dust, and water.
The people fall and acclaim YHWH.
Then revelation becomes massacre as every Baal prophet is seized and slaughtered at Kishon.
Elijah hears rain before the sky shows it.
Ahab eats while Elijah folds himself into prayer upon the mountain.
The servant looks repeatedly at an empty horizon.
A cloud no larger than a hand finally rises from the sea.
Wind, darkness, and great rain break the drought.
Elijah runs before the royal chariot toward Jezreel.

contemplative_note: The holiest resistance in the chapter may be Obadiah's hidden caves, bread, and water—not the fire or the massacre. Any spirituality that celebrates Carmel must refuse Kishon: truth does not need self-harm, religious humiliation, or slaughter to become true.
